extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students of complex analysis (and instructors using the textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter giving definitions, theorems and techniques about holomorphic functions, power series, parametrized curves, contour integration, and introductory instances of Cauchy's theorem. Targeted at students learning the foundations of complex analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic implies Cauchy–Riemann
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic at z0 then the partials of the real and imaginary parts exist and satisfy ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = −∂v/∂x (the Cauchy–Riemann equations). Equivalently ∂f/∂z̄(z0) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by taking directional limits (h real and h purely imaginary) and separating real and imaginary parts; this links complex differentiability to classical real partial derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Riemann converse (regularity hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f = u + iv is defined on an open set Ω and u and v are continuously differentiable and satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations on Ω, then f is holomorphic on Ω and f'(z) = ∂f/∂z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses first-order Taylor expansions of u and v with error terms |h|ψ(h) → 0 and shows the complex difference quotient tends to a limit; continuity of partials is essential in this converse formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex differential operators and holomorphic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Define operators ∂/∂z = 1/2(∂/∂x − i∂/∂y) and ∂/∂z̄ = 1/2(∂/∂x + i∂/∂y). A function f is holomorphic iff ∂f/∂z̄ = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operators compactly express the Cauchy–Riemann equations; the text uses them to relate real derivatives to complex derivatives and to express f'(z) in operator form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between Jacobian determinant and complex derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: If F(x,y) = f(z) with f holomorphic at z0 then det JF(x0,y0) = |f'(z0)|^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by expressing JF via the Cauchy–Riemann equations and identifying the real-linear map with multiplication by f'(z0); useful to connect complex differentiability with area-scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of power series and radius of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A power series has the form Σ_{n=0}^∞ a_n z^n (or centered Σ a_n (z−z0)^n). There exists 0 ≤ R ≤ ∞ (the radius of convergence) such that (i) the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and (ii) diverges for |z| > R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard's formula gives 1/R = lim sup |a_n|^{1/n}. On the boundary |z| = R behaviour may vary (convergence or divergence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire functions and examples (exponential, sine, cosine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: e^z = Σ z^n/n! has R = ∞ (entire). sin z and cos z have power series with infinite radius as well and satisfy Euler relations to e^{iz}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence on every disc follows from comparison with e^{|z|}; these examples illustrate power series that converge on the whole plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termwise differentiation of power series
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the disc of convergence a power series f(z) = Σ a_n z^n can be differentiated term-by-term to give f'(z) = Σ n a_n z^{n−1}, and the derived series has the same radius of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits f into partial sum polynomial SN and tail EN and shows tail contribution to difference quotient is uniformly small; Hadamard's formula and the limit n^{1/n} = 1 justify equality of radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series are C^∞ (analytic ⇒ holomorphic and conversely later)
rubrics_metrics.description: A power series defines an infinitely complex-differentiable function on its disc of convergence; higher derivatives are obtained by termwise differentiation. Analytic (power-series representable) functions are holomorphic; conversely every holomorphic function is analytic (proved later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary emphasizes that power series provide a particularly tractable class of holomorphic functions and underlies analytic continuation properties discussed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of analytic at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: f is analytic at z0 if there exists a power series Σ a_n (z−z0)^n with positive radius of convergence that equals f in a neighborhood of z0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f has power series expansion at every point of Ω then f is analytic on Ω; by Theorem 2.6 analytic ⇒ holomorphic and the converse is proved subsequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametrized curve regularity and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A parametrized curve z(t):[a,b]→C is smooth if z'(t) exists, is continuous, and z'(t) ≠ 0 on [a,b]. Piecewise-smooth means continuous with finitely many smooth subintervals. Two parametrizations are equivalent if there is a C^1 bijection t(s) with t'(s) > 0 mapping one parameter interval to the other (preserving orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence ensures the geometric curve and its orientation are well-defined independently of parametrization; right/left derivatives at endpoints interpreted as one-sided limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed and simple curve definitions; circle parametrizations
rubrics_metrics.description: A parametrized curve is closed if z(a)=z(b). A closed curve is simple if it has no self-intersections (except possibly the identification of endpoints). The positively oriented circle C_r(z0) is parametrized by z(t)=z0+re^{it}, t∈[0,2π], and the negative orientation by z0+re^{-it}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions set up orientation conventions used in integrals and later theorems such as Cauchy's integral formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of a continuous function along a curve (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ is a smooth curve parametrized by z:[a,b]→C and f is continuous on γ, define ∫_γ f(z) dz = ∫_a^b f(z(t)) z'(t) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change of variables shows this integral is independent of the chosen equivalent parametrization. For piecewise-smooth curves, the integral is the sum over smooth pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of a curve
rubrics_metrics.description: length(γ) = ∫_a^b |z'(t)| dt for a smooth parametrization z(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invariant under equivalent parametrizations; for piecewise-smooth curves, length is sum of lengths of smooth parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of contour integrals (linearity, reversal, ML inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Linearity: ∫_γ (αf + βg) = α∫_γ f + β∫_γ g. (ii) Reversal: ∫_{γ^{-}} f = −∫_γ f. (iii) Estimate: |∫_γ f(z) dz| ≤ sup_{z∈γ}|f(z)| · length(γ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linearity and reversal follow from the real integral; the third is a standard bound (often called the ML-inequality) used for estimating contour integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive (antiderivative) and path-independence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A primitive for f on Ω is a holomorphic function F with F' = f on Ω. If f has a primitive, then for any curve γ from w1 to w2 in Ω, ∫_γ f(z) dz = F(w2) − F(w1); in particular integrals over closed curves vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is by the chain rule and fundamental theorem of calculus on parametrizations; conversely vanishing integrals on appropriate classes of closed curves imply existence of primitives (used later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: nonexistence of global primitive for 1/z in C\{0}
rubrics_metrics.description: The function f(z) = 1/z has no primitive in C \\ {0}; for the unit circle C parametrized by z=e^{it}, ∫_C 1/z dz = 2πi ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example motivates the role of topology (holes) in existence of primitives and the necessity of domain hypotheses in Cauchy's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic derivative zero implies constant (Corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in a region Ω and f'(z) = 0 throughout Ω, then f is constant on Ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses path-independence: integrate f' along any curve from a fixed point to show values agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for asymptotics (O, o, ∼)
rubrics_metrics.description: f(z) = O(g(z)) means |f(z)| ≤ C|g(z)| near the point; f(z) = o(g(z)) means f/g → 0; f ∼ g means f/g → 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard asymptotic notation employed in proofs (controls error terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goursat's theorem (triangle version of Cauchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is open and T ⊂ Ω is a triangle whose interior is contained in Ω, and f is holomorphic in Ω, then ∫_T f(z) dz = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof avoids assuming continuity of f' (uses only existence of derivative). It proceeds by repeated bisection of triangles, error estimates with ψ(z)(z−z0) remainder, and letting mesh → 0 to conclude integral is 0. Goursat underlies many later results including existence of primitives in simple regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's theorem (informal statement) and Cauchy integral formula preview
rubrics_metrics.description: Loosely: if f is holomorphic in an open set Ω and γ is a closed curve whose interior is contained in Ω then ∮_γ f(z) dz = 0. Moreover, for a circle C with interior in Ω, for all z inside C one has f(z) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ (Cauchy integral formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states it as the central fact of the chapter, and indicates differentiation of the formula yields all higher-derivative formulas and regularity consequences (holomorphic ⇒ C^∞ and analytic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of primitives in a disc
rubrics_metrics.description: A holomorphic function in an open disc has a primitive in that disc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct consequence of Goursat's theorem; the theorem in the text is about to be proved (Theorem 2.1). Existence of local primitives is a key step toward proving path-independence and Cauchy's theorem in simple regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hadamard formula for radius of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The radius of convergence R of Σ a_n z^n satisfies 1/R = lim sup_{n→∞} |a_n|^{1/n} (with 1/0 = ∞, 1/∞ = 0 conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute radii for standard series (e.g., R=∞ for e^z, R=1 for geometric series) and to compare radii for f and f'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence of power series on closed discs interior to radius
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n z^n converges absolutely for some z0 then it converges uniformly on every disc |z| ≤ |z0|; in particular the exponential series converges uniformly on every disc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence on compact subdiscs justifies termwise operations such as differentiation and integration; the text uses comparison tests (|z|^n/n! ≤ e^{|z|}) to show uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for proving termwise differentiation (tail estimate method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify f'(z) = Σ n a_n z^{n−1}, split f = S_N + E_N (finite polynomial + tail), differentiate polynomial exactly, and show tail EN's difference quotient is uniformly small via an absolute-convergence tail estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses bounds |(z0+h)^n − z0^n| ≤ n r^{n−1} |h| for |z0|,|z0+h| < r and the absolute convergence of Σ n|a_n| r^{n−1} to control the tail.
